extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of constitutional law and political science (general educated readers)
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of US federal government structure
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook account of the nature, design goals, and practical operation of the United States federal government (especially the Presidency and presidential election). Intended to explain what framers sought and how institutions have worked in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vigour and efficiency
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the four objects the framers set before themselves for excellence of government. The framers sought to achieve this by creating a strong executive (see discussion of the President).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of each department
rubrics_metrics.description: The independence of each of its departments (as being essential to the permanency of its form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieved by separating legislative, executive, and judicial powers from one another, and by contrivances of checks and balances so that no one department can usurp the others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on the people
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promoted by making authorities elective and holding elections frequently so government remains answerable to the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security of individual freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The security under it of the freedom of the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protected both by checks and balances arranged to restrain any one department from tyranny and by placing certain rights of the citizen under the protection of a written constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Separating the legislative, executive, and judicial powers from one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fundamental structural principle; used alongside checks and balances to prevent concentration of power and protect permanence of the form of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances to restrain tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: The contrivance of various checks and balances ... so arranged as to restrain any one department from tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These arrangements are both preventive (limit scope of action) and corrective (allow other organs to check abuses). They also work with constitutional protections of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorities elective and frequent elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Making all authorities elective and elections frequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seen as the method to keep government dependent on the people; historical practices (state elections, national conventions) and evolution (popular election of presidential electors) illustrate implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written constitution as supreme instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: A supreme instrument expressing the will of the sovereign people, placed above and controlling the national legislature itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framers treated the Constitution as binding on Congress and the President; acts beyond constitutional powers are void and may be treated as such by citizens and courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong single executive (President)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation of a single head of the executive to secure promptitude, vigour, and continuous policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framers preferred a single magistrate (modelled on State governors and restrained versions of the British king) to remedy feebleness of Congress under the Confederation. Debate existed (Hamilton urged life tenure for stability; rejected). Practical constraints (four-year term, Senate's role in treaties/appointments, impeachment) were used to limit abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential independence and non-partisan dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: The President was meant to stand apart from and above political parties and to represent the nation as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design features intended to promote this: short salary (to avoid corruption), prohibition of titles of nobility, limited federal patronage, four-year term rather than life, and the original electoral mechanism intended to produce electors chosen for personal merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral College method of presidential selection (double election)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each State chooses a number of presidential electors equal to the number of its representatives in both Houses of Congress; electors meet in their States on a day fixed by law and give their votes in writing for President and Vice‑President; votes are sealed and transmitted to the capital and opened by the President of the Senate in the presence of both Houses and counted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional procedure intended to have deliberative, qualified electors choose the chief magistrate; includes the requirement that electors not be members of Congress nor holders of any Federal office to preserve independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electors' independence (original intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Electors were intended to be chosen 'on account of their personal merits' and to exercise independent judgment in selecting the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original expectation: electors would be better qualified than the masses. Practical anti-pattern: electors became party agents, selected under party pledges and effectively rubber-stamping popular choices; described as a 'mere cog‑wheel' in modern practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: State discretion over method of choosing electors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution leaves the method of choosing electors to each State (some States originally appointed electors by legislature; others adopted popular vote; variations included district vs general ticket systems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical evolution: early legislatures chose electors in some States; by mid‑19th century direct popular vote and the general‑ticket system became dominant; States can still change methods (examples: South Carolina, Michigan, Colorado noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Winner‑take‑all (general ticket) effects and focus on doubtful states
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing electors by the general ticket over the whole State usually causes the whole weight of a State to be thrown into the scale of one candidate, concentrating the contest in doubtful (swing) States and making campaigning languid in safe States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 1884 New York's 36 electoral votes decided the national result despite a narrow state margin; consequence is national campaigns concentrate on a few competitive States and many popular votes in large losing-state minorities are effectively 'lost'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of President elected by minority of popular votes
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Electoral College/winner‑take‑all arrangement a candidate may be elected President while receiving fewer popular votes nationwide than another candidate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples given: 1876 (Hayes behind Tilden by ~252,000 votes) and 1888 (Harrison behind Cleveland by 95,534 votes). This is a foreseeable effect of state‑based electoral allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure if no electoral majority (House choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: If no candidate receives a majority of the whole number of electors appointed, the choice goes to the House of Representatives, which chooses from among the three candidates with the largest electoral vote totals; the House votes by States and a majority of States is necessary for choice; if no choice is made the Vice‑President becomes President (if one was chosen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the 1800 election (tie between Jefferson and Burr) which was resolved by the House after long struggle; only twice has the election gone to the House. The House method and state‑vote aggregation can lead to deadlock if delegations are evenly split.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two‑term tradition for Presidents (informal limit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Constitution prescribes no limit on re‑eligibility, a practice/tradition (established by Washington) of declining to seek more than two terms developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two‑term custom governed presidential behavior for a long time; attempts to break it (e.g., movement for Grant's third term, Roosevelt's later break via party schism in 1912) show it was tradition rather than law until the 20th century.
